analysis.one_liner: Denies tax deductions for executive pay above $1 million or 25 times the median worker's pay.
analysis.headline: Sens. Gillibrand and Durbin introduced the bill in September 2017, but the Senate Finance Committee never acted on it and it died when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rewritten the tax code so companies could not deduct executive pay above $1 million or 25 times what their median employee makes, whichever is lower. It would also have required shareholder approval for any pay above that line, made companies report their lowest, median, and highest pay, and fined companies that paid over the cap without approval. The Finance Committee took no action, and the bill died there.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, shareholders would gain more say over top executive pay, taxpayers would gain because companies could no longer write off extreme pay packages as a business expense, and rank-and-file employees would gain from pay-disclosure reports that show exactly how far their pay sits from the top.

how_it_helps.text: Companies would lose the tax deduction for any employee's pay above the lesser of $1 million or 25 times the median employee pay, so ordinary taxpayers would stop subsidizing extreme pay packages through the tax code.

Companies could only pay above the cap if at least 50% of shareholders approved the package in a vote where proxy materials show the lowest, median, and highest employee pay, giving owners a direct say.

The Securities and Exchange Commission could fine companies the full amount of the excessive pay if they paid over the cap without shareholder approval, and those fines could not be deducted from taxes.
Each company paying excessive compensation would have to file a report showing its lowest-paid, highest-paid, and median employee pay and how many employees exceed the cap, making pay gaps visible.

analysis.who_pays: Large publicly traded companies and their highest-paid executives, who would face higher effective tax bills, new compliance and reporting duties, shareholder votes on big pay packages, and SEC fines equal to any pay above the cap that lacked approval.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large corporations and their top executives

drawbacks.text: The cap applies to any employee, not just CEOs, so the blunt formula could hit legitimate cases where a handful of people earn far more than a large, mostly part-time or seasonal workforce, since the bill counts part-time and seasonal staff in the median.

Companies would have ways around the cap: they could hold nominal shareholder votes that management-controlled insiders carry, or restructure pay into forms the law treats differently, so the payoff for ordinary taxpayers might be smaller than it appears.
The reporting and shareholder-vote requirements would add compliance costs for companies, which are often passed along to consumers or shareholders.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real but modest: ending the tax deduction for extreme pay and giving shareholders a vote would narrow pay gaps and raise some revenue, at the price of compliance costs and a formula that can misfire at companies with unusual pay structures. The formula's dependence on a company's own median pay also creates a loophole incentive — keeping low-paid work off the payroll raises the cap.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Sens. Gillibrand and Durbin introduced the bill on September 19, 2017, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance.
No further action was ever recorded; the Finance Committee held no markup and the full Senate never voted on it.
The bill died when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.
Only one senator besides the sponsor signed on, so the bill never built the support needed to force committee action.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large corporations and their top executives, who keep the tax deduction for pay above $1 million and face no shareholder-approval requirement or pay-gap reporting.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large corporations and their top executives

for.name: Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the Senate.

for.name: Sen. Richard Durbin
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill at introduction as its only cosponsor.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never scheduled a markup or vote on it.

against.name: Orrin Hatch
against.what_they_did: As committee chair during the 115th Congress, never brought the bill to a markup or vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Both the sponsor and its single cosponsor were Democrats; the bill drew no Republican support, but it also never reached a vote, so the chamber's partisan divide was never tested.

industries.industry: Large public corporations and their top executives
industries.note: The bill would end their tax deduction for pay above $1 million or 25 times median employee pay and subject big packages to shareholder votes and SEC fines. Their interest in keeping pay uncapped and fully deductible ran against the taxpayers and shareholders footing the bill.

industries.industry: Compensation consulting and payroll administration firms
industries.note: New median-pay calculations, annual reports to the IRS and SEC, and shareholder votes would create billable compliance work, while capping executive pay could shrink the market for designing large packages.
